## Generalized Linear Model

### POISSON \_ DELETE

This section was lead by Benjamin Jud.\
Using a Poisson Generalized Linear Model, we will examine count data on arrivals and overnights in xxx...\
\
First, lets examine the two columns:

```{r}
summary(swiss_hotel_panel[, c("arrivals", "overnights")])
```

From the summary call, we can see that both columns consist of integer values greater than 0. As such, we can model this count data using poisson and quasi-poisson models. We can also see that there is quite data is generally left skewed, with a long right-sided tail. As such, both `Arrivals` and `Overnights` will be log-transformed.

```{r}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
hist(log(swiss_hotel_panel$arrivals), main = 'Histogram of Arrivals', xlab = 'Arrivals (log transformed)')
hist(log(swiss_hotel_panel$overnights), main = 'Histogram of Overnights', xlab = 'Overnights (log transformed)')
```

```{r}
glm_arrivals = glm(arrivals ~ ., 
                   data = swiss_hotel_panel,
                   family = 'quasipoisson')
summary(glm_arrivals)

```

### Binomial

Using a Binomial Generalized Linear Model, we will attempt to model and predict growth from any specific market, based on xxx

The following is an overview of grow, where `1` represents a year-over-year increase in hotel stays from that particular market, and `0` represents a decline in hotel stays.

```{r}
n_growth = tapply(swiss_hotel_panel$growth == 1, swiss_hotel_panel$year, sum, na.rm = TRUE)

yoy_growth = as.numeric(n_growth) / as.numeric(table(swiss_hotel_panel$year))
```

```{r}
years = as.numeric(colnames(tbl_growth))

plot(years, yoy_growth, type = "b", pch = 16,
     xlab = "Year", ylab = "Share with YoY growth",
     main = "YoY Growth in Hotel Stays", xaxt = "n")
axis(1, at = years)
```

First, we split our data into a training and testing set such that we can later run a prediction against the model, and validate our outcomes. We will be using a split of 70% (training) and 30% (testing).

```{r}

glm_sample_rows = sample.int(nrow(swiss_hotel_panel), floor(0.7 * nrow(swiss_hotel_panel)))

glm_train_dataset <- swiss_hotel_panel[glm_sample_rows, ]   
glm_test_dataset  <- swiss_hotel_panel[-glm_sample_rows, ]  
```

Now, we will construct a binomial GLM Model to find factors that contribute to this growth.

```{r}
##not sure how many vars you can include in one of these
glm.growth = glm(growth ~ 
                  gdp_growth_origin
                 +real_fx_index
                 +rel_income
                 +visa_required
                 +origin_group
                 +year,
                 data = glm_train_dataset,
                 family = 'binomial')
summary(glm.growth)
```

#### Predicting Growth from Origin Country GDP Growth

```{r}
glm.growth_origin = glm(growth~gdp_growth_origin, data = glm_train_dataset, family = 'binomial')
plot(glm_train_dataset$gdp_growth_origin, glm_train_dataset$growth)
```
